name: Methyldienolone (M-Dien)
lead: Methyldienolone (developmental code RU-3467, also called M-Dien) is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid, a 17-alpha-methylated derivative of 19-nortestosterone related to dienolone.[1] It has not been marketed as a medicine. Bodybuilders who discussed it in the 2000s were interested in it as an oral androgen for adding muscle size and strength, and for a harder, leaner look while cutting.[2][3]

Published literature is sparse. Wikipedia lists it as a US Schedule III substance and as prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency, and the research that exists concerns detection chemistry and environmental breakdown products rather than human use.[1][4][5]

T Nation members in 2004 described mixed results: one said it seemed hit or miss from person to person, while another reported lackluster gains on a lean bulk but thought it might suit cutting.[2][3] A later member advised against old prohormones including methyldienolone because of potency concerns.[6]

paras: Methyldienolone is 17-alpha-methyl-19-nor-delta-9-testosterone, with a molecular formula of C19H26O2. Its 17-alpha alkyl group is the feature that allows oral activity in steroids of this kind, and Wikipedia also categorizes it among hepatotoxic compounds.[1]

In the United States it is Schedule III under the Controlled Substances Act, and it appears on the World Anti-Doping Agency list of prohibited substances.[1] A 2026 study identified new metabolites using human liver microsomes and mass spectrometry for doping-control purposes.[5] Federal-law discussions on T Nation in 2003 and 2008 listed it among the newly scheduled anabolic steroids.[7]

Methyldienolone was discussed on T Nation around 2004 to 2009 alongside other orals and prohormones. One 2004 poster described it as real steroid with limited feedback, saying results seemed to vary by person [2]. Another poster reported lackluster gains with two brands during a lean bulk and suggested it might be better for cutting [3]. A 2009 thread asked why it was reported to be liver toxic at very small amounts [8]. A 2018 reply advised against it because of its potency and designer-steroid status [6].

No studies found. Related laboratory work includes an environmental chemistry study of photolysis products of methyldienolone and dienogest, which found products with progestogenic and androgenic activity weaker than the parents,[4] and a 2026 study identifying metabolites with human liver microsomes for doping control.[5]

lore.intro: Methyldienolone appears in 2000s T Nation threads on oral steroids and prohormones, mainly as a compound with variable reported results.[2][3][8]

claims.claim: M-Dien gives muscle and strength gains as an oral androgen
claims.believers: Some posters called it a real steroid and others said it might be good for cutting, though results were described as varying by person.[2][3]
claims.experts: No published human studies have examined its effects on muscle; the literature covers chemistry and detection.[4][5]

claims.believers: A 2009 poster asked about reports that it was liver toxic even at very small amounts, and a 2018 reply cited its potency as a reason to avoid it.[8][6]
claims.experts: Wikipedia categorizes it among hepatotoxins, and 17-alpha-alkylated steroids as a class are associated with liver effects; no human data specific to this compound were found.[1]

card.summary: An unmarketed oral 19-nor androgen; almost nothing published beyond detection chemistry.
card.note: Prohibited in sport; no human data found.

quick.overview:
Methyldienolone is an oral 19-nortestosterone derivative that was never marketed as a drug.

The literature consists of chemistry and doping-control papers.
quick.mechanism: It is classed as an androgen receptor agonist; no pharmacokinetic detail was found.
quick.risks: No adverse-effect data were found. It is prohibited in sport and listed as Schedule III in the US per Wikipedia.

chain: Claimed muscle size, strength and leanness
angle.text: Users discussed methyldienolone as an oral androgen for muscle growth and a leaner, harder look on a cut. No human trials describe these effects.
